lessons.introduction: Start with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript basics. Draw your first object, then explain time-based rotation and local/world positions. Coordinates, axes, and angles are introduced here; WebGL and matrix calculations are not prerequisites. Each starter is an independent HTML document. Predict, edit one value, run, and record the observed numbers and reasons in the site notes. Reading a step or explanation does not replace your code; loading an example is a separate action.

steps.title: Draw a scene on a canvas
steps.explanation:
The starter is an HTML document with canvas and output elements. Inline style sets the canvas display size; JavaScript inside script type="module" draws the image. import * as THREE from 'three' exposes the library names under THREE. The site supplies the module, so no npm installation or external server is required.

document.querySelector('canvas') finds the canvas element in the document. output is selected in the same way; assigning a string to output.textContent displays it as text.

The canvas is the HTML element that receives the image. Scene groups 3D objects and Camera sets the viewing position and direction. WebGLRenderer uses them when renderer.render(scene, camera) draws to the canvas. Scene and Camera are not HTML elements. new creates an object; renderer.render(...) calls a method on an existing object.

Find canvas, scene, camera, and renderer in order. Check that the renderer receives the canvas selected from HTML. The camera is at (0, 0, 5), looking at the origin. There are no objects yet, so a background-only image is expected. In scene.background = new THREE.Color('#edf2f7'), change only the color to '#172554' and run. Record your prediction first.

draw reads canvas.clientWidth and clientHeight in CSS px. A zero width or height returns early to defer drawing. When you reopen the preview, ResizeObserver reports the size change and calls draw. observe(canvas) starts observation. At a positive size, setSize(w, h, false) fits the image, while camera.aspect = w / h and updateProjectionMatrix() apply the camera ratio. false leaves the CSS size intact. This supporting code appears in every step; keep it unchanged here. The next unit explores sizing, buffers, and DPR.

The + operators join strings and numbers in output. The canvas and output selectors each find one element in this document. Client dimensions are integers including padding but excluding borders and scrollbars; this canvas has zero padding and border. Observation and animation continue while the document remains mounted; running again replaces the iframe.
steps.solutionExplanation: scene.background is independent of the body background CSS. A changed value may leave an existing image unchanged until render runs again. If even the background is missing, read output and the error display, then check script execution, the canvas connection, and render in order.
steps.expected: The empty scene background changes from #edf2f7 to #172554. output shows the actual display width and height. Having no cube yet is expected.
hints: Check that the selected HTML canvas and the canvas in WebGLRenderer({ canvas }) are the same element.
After changing scene.background, check for renderer.render(scene, camera).
Assign new THREE.Color('#172554') to scene.background and render again.
questions: What do canvas, Scene, Camera, and WebGLRenderer each do?
Are scene.background and the body background CSS the same value?

steps.title: Your first cube and camera
steps.explanation:
This independent starter includes a cube. geometry = new THREE.BoxGeometry(1, 1, 1) defines its shape; material = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: '#2563eb' }) defines the surface; cube = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material) combines them into a scene object. This material is visible without lights, so no light is added.

Change only color in the material constructor and run. Then keep the color and change cube.position.x from 0 to 1. position is relative to the parent, initially Scene. With this camera, +X appears rightward and +Y upward, but screen directions depend on camera orientation. Temporarily comment out scene.add(cube), run, and restore it. Creation and scene connection are separate operations.

Restore cube.position.x to 0 and change the last argument of camera.position.set(0, 0, 5) to 7, changing camera.position.z from 5 to 7. Predict the cube's appearance from the more distant camera. Now change camera.position.set(0, 0, 5) to camera.position.set(2, 0, 5), keeping camera.lookAt(0, 0, 0). position sets location; lookAt sets the direction toward a world-space target. A camera initially looks along local -Z. lookAt does not move it to the target.

The completed example shows the final comparison: an orange cube and camera=(2, 0, 5). Test the intermediate x=1, z=7, and removed add separately in the starter, restoring each before the next test.
steps.solutionExplanation: create a Mesh from geometry and material, connect it to Scene, and render with a Camera that can see it. When z changes from 5 to 7 the perspective image is smaller, but the geometry width remains 1. near=.1 and far=50 define the drawing depth range. Keep them here; unit 03 explores clipping. If you place the camera inside the cube, do not mistake the blank image for missing lighting.
steps.expected: color changes the surface color; cube.position.x changes location. Removing add hides the cube. It appears smaller at camera.z=7. After lookAt, camera.position remains (2, 0, 5).
hints: Find Mesh creation and scene.add(cube) separately. Creation alone does not connect it to Scene.
Restore the cube to the origin and check that camera.z is 5 or 7.
Check location, direction, and drawing with camera.position.set(2, 0, 5); camera.lookAt(0, 0, 0); renderer.render(scene, camera);
questions: Why is a created Mesh invisible if it is never added?
What do position and lookAt each change?
Does moving the camera farther away change geometry width?

steps.title: Turn time into rotation
steps.explanation:
The starter contains the cube and camera and begins with speed=0, so it is stationary. Passing renderFrame(timeMs) to renderer.setAnimationLoop makes the renderer call it each frame. A function passed for later invocation is called a callback.

timeMs is a timestamp in milliseconds. Save its first value in start and calculate elapsed seconds with seconds = (timeMs - start) / 1000. In cube.rotation.y = seconds * speed, speed is in rad/s. rotation uses radians: Math.PI is 180°, Math.PI / 2 is 90°, and 2 * Math.PI is one turn. Remember that camera.fov uses degrees instead.

Set speed to .5, run again, and read angle when output seconds is near 2. Run again with speed=1 and compare near the same 2 seconds. A frame might not occur at exactly 2 seconds; record the actual time and angle together. Adding a fixed angle per frame can make rotation per second depend on display refresh rate. This example calculates the angle from time.

renderFrame calls draw(). renderer.render(scene, camera) inside draw paints the updated rotation. Repeated calls reuse the same objects.
steps.solutionExplanation: .5rad/s for 2 seconds gives 1rad; 1rad/s for 2 seconds gives 2rad. Without converting 2000ms into seconds, the angle is 1000 times larger. renderer.render(scene, camera) must also run inside renderFrame after changing rotation. The same cube is updated, rather than recreated each frame. renderer.setAnimationLoop(null) stops repeated calls.
steps.expected: speed=0 is stationary. Near 2 seconds, speed=.5 gives angle≈1rad and speed=1 gives angle≈2rad. Both output and image change.
hints: Check whether seconds and angle both change. If only the numbers change, inspect render placement.
Check the division of timeMs by 1000 and the rad/s unit of speed.
Inside renderFrame, call renderer.render(scene, camera) after cube.rotation.y = seconds * speed.
questions: How does adding a fixed angle per frame differ from seconds*speed?
Why divide timeMs by 1000?
What should you check if numbers change but the image is still?

steps.title: Compare parent and child positions
steps.explanation:
This independent starter is stationary, with no animation. parent = new THREE.Group() is a parent node without its own shape. parent.position=(0, 0, 0), child.position=(2, 0, 0), and parent.add(child), scene.add(parent) connect them. The camera looks at the origin from (5, 4, 7) so that XZ motion is visible.

The tree is Scene → parent Group → child Mesh. child.position is local to parent; world position includes parent transforms in the coordinate system of the whole scene. angleInput has a string value, so convert it with Number(angleInput.value) before assigning parent.rotation.y. The choices are radian values 0 and Math.PI / 2.

world = new THREE.Vector3() stores the result. child.getWorldPosition(world) writes into world without modifying child.position. Predict both positions at rotation 0, then run: both are (2, 0, 0). Change parent Y rotation to Math.PI / 2 and compare again. Expect local=(2, 0, 0), world=(0, 0, -2). Point your right thumb along +Y; your curled fingers indicate positive rotation. In the XZ diagram, +X turns toward -Z.

The HTML range input has two values: 0 and 1.5707963267948966, the latter equal to Math.PI / 2. addEventListener('input', draw) calls draw when the value changes. toFixed(2) formats a number as a string with two decimal places. coordinates groups x/y/z for display without changing the position.
steps.solutionExplanation:
parent rotation turns the axes used to express the child's position. The child remains 2 units along the parent's +X. getWorldPosition applies the current parent transforms without requiring manual matrix multiplication. Values such as 1e-16 are floating-point results close to 0. Format output to 2 decimal places without rounding the actual position.

An object has only one parent. scene.add(child) after parent.add(child) removes child from parent. Record your predictions, actual coordinates, and reasons for both rotation conditions in the site notes.
steps.expected: parent stays at the origin. At parent.rotation.y=0, world=(2, 0, 0); at Math.PI / 2, world≈(0, 0, -2). child local=(2, 0, 0) is unchanged.
hints: Read child.position and world together in output and identify the value relative to the parent.
Check that the final connection is parent.add(child). scene.add(child) changes the parent.
Read with const world = new THREE.Vector3(); child.getWorldPosition(world);. Changing only parent.rotation.y to Math.PI / 2 gives local=(2, 0, 0), world=(0, 0, -2).
questions: Why is child.position unchanged when only the parent rotates?
Does getWorldPosition(world) modify child.position?
What changes if scene.add(child) is called last?

lessons.introduction: Match CSS display size, drawing buffer size, and camera aspect as separate concerns. Each independent HTML starter contains a front-facing BoxGeometry(1, 1, .2) and does not require previous code. stage has no padding/border; canvas uses display:block; width:100%; height:100%. The 240×240 and 480×240 conditions are examples when space permits. On narrow screens max-width can limit them; use actual w,h from output. Record shape proportions, CSS size, buffer size, and DPR in the site notes. Predict before running, change one item at a time, and use the site notes: conditions / prediction / actual image and numbers / reason for differences. The site supplies the three import; no separate installation is needed.

steps.title: Display size and buffer size
steps.explanation:
Initially DPR=1 and camera.aspect=1 in a square stage. renderer.setSize runs only once at startup. The camera looks from (0, 0, 5) toward the origin; the box has no rotation, making its front-face proportions easy to observe.

Use the size button to increase only stage width, then read CSS and buffer dimensions. stage.clientWidth/clientHeight use CSS px; canvas.width/height use buffer px. CSS can display the old buffer image over a wider area without drawing additional pixels. A changed display ratio can stretch the square horizontally.

In every example startWhenVisible uses requestAnimationFrame to wait for the first positive size, calls resizeScene once, then stops. A callback is a function the browser invokes before a later repaint; return ends this function call. This bootstrap does not observe later changes. addEventListener runs a function on click; assigning a CSS length string to stage.style.width changes display width only. reportSize reads current client and buffer dimensions and displays them through output.textContent. querySelector finds HTML elements; renderer.domElement is the same canvas supplied from HTML. In output, toFixed(4) formats a number as a string with four decimal places; + joins strings. Buffer pixel count is canvas.width × canvas.height.
steps.solutionExplanation: with a 240×240 buffer displayed at 480×240, the same image is stretched 2 times horizontally. If actual width differs from 480, substitute the output values. Read the actual stage size rather than body or window width. Automatic resizing is intentionally absent in this step.
steps.expected: stage width changes while canvas.width/height keep their initial values. The square can appear stretched. On narrow screens target and measured dimensions can differ.
hints: Read the CSS px and buffer px output rows separately.
Compare whether canvas.width changes after changing stage width.
Displaying a 240×240 buffer at 480×240 stretches it 2 times horizontally. Calculate the same ratio from your actual output.
questions: Does changing CSS width always change buffer width?
Why can stage width differ from window width?

steps.title: Match the buffer and camera separately
steps.explanation:
The starter resizeScene() reads w=stage.clientWidth, h=stage.clientHeight and calls renderer.setSize(w, h, false). The size button calls it, but camera.aspect is still 1. Choose a wide size and check that buffer dimensions match display dimensions. The square can still appear stretched.

After setSize in resizeScene(), add camera.aspect = w / h; camera.updateProjectionMatrix();. Compare the same sizes again. aspect is width/height; updateProjectionMatrix applies that ratio to projection calculations. Changing only one is insufficient.
steps.solutionExplanation: matching the buffer determines how many pixels are drawn. Camera projection determines the proportions used to place objects into that pixel region. With fixed vertical FOV, a wider view shows more of the scene horizontally without flattening objects. false in setSize prevents CSS display-size changes, not buffer changes.
steps.expected: setSize alone matches the buffer but can leave shape proportions wrong. Updating aspect and projection together preserves the front-face proportions.
hints: Compare display w/h with camera.aspect.
Check for updateProjectionMatrix after assigning camera.aspect.
Use renderer.setSize(w, h, false); camera.aspect = w / h; camera.updateProjectionMatrix(); before rendering.
questions: Why can a shape stretch even when the buffer size matches?
What does false prevent in the third setSize argument?

steps.title: Observe element size changes
steps.explanation:
This independent starter includes the completed resizeScene(). Now the size button only changes CSS and no longer calls resizeScene directly. The initial frame matches, but later stage changes do not.

Create observer = new ResizeObserver(resizeScene) and connect observer.observe(stage). ResizeObserver is a browser Web API, not Three.js. It calls the callback when an observed element changes size. Keep the initial resizeScene() call to size the first frame immediately.

Leave window dimensions unchanged and press the stage size button. The observer responds to the element's own size changes. Observe stage, which defines the size, rather than canvas. stage has no padding/border and canvas fills it at 100%, making the measurement basis clear.
steps.solutionExplanation: the observer does not understand cameras or buffers automatically. The resizeScene callback performs setSize, aspect and projection updates, and rendering. If dimensions oscillate, check false in setSize, canvas CSS, and that stage is observed. Use observer.disconnect() when observation ends.
steps.expected: Changing only the stage button matches measured dimensions, buffer, and aspect without resizing the browser window. resizeScene redraws the image too.
hints: Check output to see whether changing only stage CSS runs resizeScene.
Check that observer.observe receives stage rather than canvas.
Connect const observer = new ResizeObserver(resizeScene); observer.observe(stage); resizeScene();.
questions: Why can a window resize listener be insufficient?
Does the observer itself call render?

steps.title: Compare DPR 1 and 2
steps.explanation:
The starter includes resizing and starts with dpr=1. output displays actual CSS w,h, canvas.width/height, camera.aspect, and dpr. Change dpr to 2 and call renderer.setPixelRatio(dpr) followed by renderer.setSize(w, h, false). w,h must be CSS dimensions, not values already multiplied by DPR.

For a 240×240 CSS display, DPR 1 gives a 240×240 buffer and DPR 2 gives 480×480. Pixel count rises from 57,600 to 230,400, a factor of 4. For other display dimensions, use actual w,h. camera.aspect remains w/h without DPR multiplication.

The input value is a string, so Number(input.value) converts it to a number. The change event runs when the selection changes. Add renderer.setPixelRatio(dpr); at the DPR comment in resizeScene, then compare input values 1 and 2.
steps.solutionExplanation: DPR affects buffer resolution along both axes. It does not request making CSS display size or scene-object size 2 times larger. Although devicePixelRatio can vary by device or browser zoom, this experiment explicitly uses 1 and 2. A sharpness difference may be subtle and processing time is not necessarily 4 times greater. Multiplying DPR 2 times gives a factor of 4 along each buffer axis; inspect setSize arguments if that happens.
steps.expected: CSS size and camera.aspect stay unchanged. At DPR 2 each buffer axis becomes 2 times larger and pixel count becomes 4 times larger. A 240×240 display gives a 480×480 buffer.
hints: Record CSS px and buffer px side by side and calculate each axis ratio.
Check whether setSize receives w*dpr, h*dpr by mistake.
In renderer.setPixelRatio(2); renderer.setSize(w, h, false);, w,h are measured CSS dimensions. camera.aspect is w/h.
questions: Why does DPR 2 give 4 times as many pixels?
Should DPR also multiply camera.aspect?
Does 4 times as many pixels guarantee 4 times the processing time?

steps.title: Hide and show the stage
steps.explanation:
The starter has buttons to hide and show stage. After reading w,h near the start of resizeScene(), check if (w === 0 || h === 0) return;. output reports hidden dimensions without claiming a newly valid aspect.

Hide and show stage. With display:none, client dimensions can be 0. Do not divide w/h when h=0 or substitute 1 and label the result normal. The observer keeps watching stage and calls resizeScene when it has size again.

stage.hidden is a boolean property controlling visibility. Buttons and output are outside stage, so they remain usable while it is hidden. The hidden output aspect is the last valid value, not a newly computed ratio.
steps.solutionExplanation: return skips this size update. It does not disconnect the observer or terminate the program. After showing, setSize and aspect use the actual dimensions and render restores the image. To finish, record shape proportions and numbers for square/wide, DPR 1/2, and recovery from hiding.
steps.expected: Hidden dimensions are reported as 0 without division by 0. Showing stage restores finite aspect and current buffer dimensions while preserving shape proportions.
hints: Read whether stage.clientWidth/clientHeight become 0 while hidden.
Check that the zero-size guard precedes w/h.
Place setSize, aspect, projection, and render after if (w === 0 || h === 0) return;. The observer calls the same function after showing.
questions: How does replacing 0 with 1 differ from skipping an update?
Why can the image recover after the function returned?

apis.description: Constructor for a scene root. Scene inherits Object3D and connects children with add. Its background member defaults to null.
apis.result: Returns a new Scene. Construction alone does not draw to a canvas.
cautions: Scene is not an HTML element.

apis.description: Constructor for a color object. This course uses CSS hex strings only.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: A CSS hex color string, such as '#edf2f7'.

apis.result: Returns a new Color.
cautions: Color spaces and linear RGB calculations are later topics.

apis.description: Constructor for a renderer that draws WebGL2 scenes to a canvas. domElement refers to its actual output canvas.

parameters.name: canvas
parameters.description: The canvas selected from HTML. Omitting it creates a new canvas.

parameters.name: antialias
parameters.description: Requests edge antialiasing at construction.

apis.result: Returns a renderer. domElement is a canvas reference, not a method.
cautions: WebGL2 support is required. Pass your existing canvas to use it.
apis.example:
const renderer = new THREE.WebGLRenderer({ canvas, antialias: true });
const actualCanvas = renderer.domElement;

apis.description: Instance method that sets renderer logical size and viewport. It also resizes the canvas buffer using DPR.

parameters.name: width
parameters.description: Logical width in CSS px.

parameters.name: height
parameters.description: Logical height in CSS px.

parameters.name: updateStyle
parameters.description: When true, also changes canvas inline CSS width and height.

apis.result: No return value. The buffer becomes floor(width*DPR) × floor(height*DPR).
cautions: Use false when CSS manages display size. Do not pass dimensions already multiplied by DPR.

apis.description: Instance method that draws the scene through a camera onto the current canvas.

parameters.name: scene
parameters.description: The scene to draw.

parameters.name: camera
parameters.description: The camera defining position, direction, and projection.

apis.result: No return value. Updates the current image.
cautions: Changing object properties does not automatically call this method.

apis.description: Constructor for a perspective camera, where distant objects appear smaller. Arguments are positional.

parameters.name: fov
parameters.description: Vertical field of view in degrees.

parameters.name: aspect
parameters.description: Display width divided by height.

parameters.name: near
parameters.description: Depth of the near plane in front of the camera.

parameters.name: far
parameters.description: Depth of the far plane.

apis.result: Returns a new PerspectiveCamera.
cautions: Set near>0 and far>near. fov uses degrees rather than the radians used by rotation.
Call updateProjectionMatrix after changing fov/aspect/near/far/zoom.
apis.example: const camera = new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(50, w / h, .1, 50);

apis.description: Constructor for a box centered at the origin, with edges parallel to local X/Y/Z.

parameters.name: width
parameters.description: Length along local X.

parameters.name: height
parameters.description: Length along local Y.

parameters.name: depth
parameters.description: Length along local Z.

apis.result: Returns a new BoxGeometry.
cautions: Segment arguments are omitted here and each defaults to 1. Editing parameters.width does not rebuild vertices.

apis.description: Constructor for a surface appearance unaffected by lights.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: The examples use CSS hex strings.

parameters.name: wireframe
parameters.description: When true, displays triangle edges.

apis.result: Returns a new material.
cautions: If this material is invisible, check Scene connection, camera, and render before adding lights.

apis.description: Constructor for a scene object combining geometry and material.

parameters.name: geometry
parameters.description: The shape object.

parameters.name: material
parameters.description: The surface appearance object.

apis.result: Returns a new Mesh without adding it to Scene.
cautions: This course supplies both arguments rather than relying on omitted defaults.
apis.example:
const cube = new THREE.Mesh(geometry, material);
scene.add(cube);

apis.description: position is a Vector3 member holding a position relative to the parent. position.set is a Vector3 method that changes its components.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Position along the parent X axis.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Position along the parent Y axis.

parameters.name: z
parameters.description: Position along the parent Z axis.

apis.result: position initially is (0, 0, 0). set mutates it and returns the same Vector3.
cautions: Change x/y/z or use set; do not replace position with an array.

apis.description: Method that points a camera toward a world-space target.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Target world X. An overload accepts a single Vector3.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Target world Y.

parameters.name: z
parameters.description: Target world Z.

apis.result: No return value. Changes camera rotation without moving its position.
cautions: Non-uniformly scaled parents are unsupported. With controls, avoid having lookAt and controls.update overwrite orientation each frame.

apis.description: Method that connects other Object3D instances as children.

parameters.name: children
parameters.description: Children to connect. Multiple arguments are accepted.

apis.result: Returns the parent itself. Children are removed from their previous parents.
cautions: An object has one parent. Its local transform is retained, but its world position is not guaranteed to stay the same.

apis.description: Euler member holding an Object3D local rotation. x/y/z are angles in radians.
apis.result: Initial angles are (0, 0, 0), with default order XYZ. Assigning components mutates the object.
cautions: Math.PI / 2 is 90°. Do not confuse radians with camera.fov degrees.
A child rotation.y is not always a rotation about world Y.

apis.description: Method that registers or stops a callback for each frame.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: The first callback argument in this non-XR example is timestamp timeMs. null stops the loop.

apis.result: No return value. The registered callback runs repeatedly.
cautions: The timestamp is in ms; elapsed seconds are (timeMs-start)/1000.
After changing object values inside the callback, also call render.

apis.description: Constructor for an Object3D node that groups child transforms. It has no shape of its own.
apis.result: Returns a new Group. position/rotation/add follow Object3D contracts.
cautions: Adding a Group does not create visible geometry.

apis.description: Constructor for an object with x/y/z components, used here to store position results.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: X component.

parameters.name: y
parameters.description: Y component.

parameters.name: z
parameters.description: Z component.

apis.result: Returns a new Vector3.
cautions: The Vector3 type does not determine whether a value is local or world-space; its use does.

apis.description: Method that reads world position including current parent transforms.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The destination object for the result; it is required.

apis.result: Mutates and returns target without changing object.position.
cautions: In 0.186.1, the method updates the required parent world matrices internally. No manual matrix multiplication is needed.

apis.description: Method that applies changed fov/aspect/near/far/zoom values to the projection matrix. Orthographic cameras expose the same method.
apis.result: No return value. The next render uses the updated projection.
cautions: Property assignment does not call this automatically.
Distinguish camera movement from changes to projection values.

apis.description: DOM members for display and buffer dimensions. clientWidth/clientHeight use CSS px; canvas.width/height use buffer px. The same Element clientWidth/clientHeight contract applies to canvas.
apis.result: Property reads yield dimension numbers. Client dimensions are integers and include padding but exclude borders. The corresponding scrollbar is also excluded.
cautions: These are Web APIs, not Three.js APIs. packageVersion records the lesson Three.js version.
The example stage has no padding/border. Do not mix direct canvas buffer assignments with renderer size management.
Display-size sources: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/clientWidth and https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element/clientHeight

apis.description: Web API that reports element size changes through a callback, including stage changes without window resizing.

parameters.name: callback
parameters.description: Function called for size changes; the example passes resizeScene.

parameters.name: target
parameters.description: The stage element observed with observe(target).

apis.result: The constructor returns an observer. observe and disconnect return no value. disconnect stops observation.
cautions: This is not a Three.js API. packageVersion records the lesson Three.js version.
Return before division if w or h is 0. An observer does not replace render.

apis.description: Method that sets buffer pixels per CSS pixel. getPixelRatio() takes no arguments and returns the currently configured ratio as a number.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The experiment explicitly uses 1 or 2. The initial renderer ratio is 1.

apis.result: No return value. Resizes the buffer using the current logical size.
cautions: It does not automatically read devicePixelRatio.
A ratio of 2 affects both axes, giving 4 times as many pixels, not necessarily 4 times the processing time.
